import torch
import torch.nn as nn
torch.set_printoptions(precision=2)
class SimpleNN(nn.Module):
def __init__(self, input_size, hidden_size, num_classes):
super(SimpleNN, self).__init__()
self.fc1 = nn.Linear(input_size, hidden_size)
self.sig = nn.Sigmoid()
self.fc2 = nn.Linear(hidden_size, num_classes)
def forward(self, x):
z1 = self.fc1(x)
a1 = self.sig(z1)
z2 = self.fc2(a1)
return z2

Weights as Matrices: Equation Conventions

There are a number of different conventions for writing the linear transformation as used in a linear_layer. I use a slightly non-standard one that I believe maps better to PyTorch and the diagrams I show in class.

ConventionEquationWhere you'll see it
Bias folded inZ = Xω
(X gets a column of 1s)		Linear regression, perceptrons and SVMs
Inputs × outputsZ = Xω + bKeras/TensorFlow, many textbooks
Outputs × inputsZ = XωT + bPyTorch nn.Linear and this course

PyTorch stores one row per neuron so it reads like the math: XωT + b

import torch
class LinearLayer:
def __init__(self, n_in, n_out):
self.W = torch.randn(n_out, n_in) * (2/n_in)**0.5
self.b = torch.zeros(n_out)
def forward(self, X):
self.X = X # keep for backward
return X @ self.W.T + self.b
def backward(self, dY):
self.dW = dY.T @ self.X # dL/dW
self.db = dY.sum(dim=0) # dL/db
return dY @ self.W # dL/dX, sent back
def update(self, lr):
self.W -= lr * self.dW
self.b -= lr * self.db

class Sigmoid:
def forward(self, Z):
self.A = 1 / (1 + torch.exp(-Z)) # saved
return self.A
def backward(self, dA):
return dA * self.A * (1 - self.A) # dL/dZ
def update(self, lr):
pass # no weights to learn

class ReLU:
def forward(self, Z):
self.Z = Z # saved
return Z.clamp(min=0)
def backward(self, dA):
return dA * (self.Z > 0).float() # dL/dZ
def update(self, lr):
pass # no weights to learn

class Network:
def __init__(self, layers):
self.layers = layers
def forward(self, X):
for layer in self.layers:
X = layer.forward(X)
return X # logits
def backward(self, y_hat, y):
grad = y_hat - y # dL/dy_hat (hard-coded here)
for layer in reversed(self.layers): # chain rule
grad = layer.backward(grad) # back to front
def update(self, lr):
for layer in self.layers:
layer.update(lr)

Our network class is really just more of a wrapper than anything else, most of the work is done in the layer classes

# Last lecture's 4 games: ND points, opp. points
X = torch.tensor([[50., 43.], [22., 24.], [38., 0.], [14., 42.]]) # ND Score, Opp. Score
y = torch.tensor([[1.], [1.], [0.], [0.]]) # close = 1, not close = 0
torch.manual_seed(0)
model = Network([LinearLayer(2, 2), Sigmoid(), LinearLayer(2, 1)])
bce = torch.nn.BCELoss()
y_hat = torch.sigmoid(model.forward(X)) # P(close)
print('y_hat at epoch 0:', y_hat.flatten(), 'loss:', bce(y_hat, y))
def train(model, X, lr=0.001, epochs=1000):
for epoch in range(epochs):
y_hat = torch.sigmoid(model.forward(X))
model.backward(y_hat, y)
model.update(lr)
return torch.sigmoid(model.forward(X))
y_hat_trained = train(model, X)
print('y_hat at epoch 1000:', y_hat_trained.flatten(), 'loss:', bce(y_hat_trained, y))
Output
y_hat at epoch 0: tensor([0.5038, 0.5367, 0.4577, 0.5866]) loss: tensor(0.7008)
y_hat at epoch 1000: tensor([0.5537, 0.5523, 0.3362, 0.5538]) loss: tensor(0.6004)

Some Issues with Backprop and Activation Functions

There are some issues that appear when you start using backprop, depending on the activation functions you use.

Saturated Sigmoids:

When a neuron's Z is far from 0, the sigmoid  , so its local derivative is effectively 0 and almost no gradient gets back through it. The neuron is saturated.

Dying ReLUs:

A ReLU's local derivative is  , so a neuron that's negative on every input passes no gradient back and never updates again. The neuron is dead.

Backpropagation · Issues with Backprop22

Saturated Sigmoids

Not dissimilar to the issues with the step function, if we are too far outside of the curve of the sigmoid, we get effectively no useful gradient information from it.

Purple dots: this section's network's 8 values of Z1 (4 games × 2 neurons) on raw scores, most of them far out on the flat top.

Dying ReLUs

Similarly to the edges of a sigmoid, a ReLU gives no useful gradient information if the Z value is less than 0.

Hollow dots: the same 8 values of Z1 at the start, nearly all on the ramp. One gradient step later, all 8 are in the dead zone.

Backpropagation · Issues with Backprop26

Fixing Both: Standardize the Inputs

Standardized inputs sit on both sides of 0, so every z starts near 0: on the steep part of the sigmoid, and positive for some games, negative for others in each ReLU neuron.

The MNIST Dataset

MNIST (LeCun and others, 1998) is the classic first dataset for neural networks: 70,000 handwritten digits (60,000 to train, 10,000 to test), each a 28 × 28 grayscale image. Flattened, that's the 784 inputs of the exam network we just did.

EMNIST (Cohen and others, 2017) adds letters in the same format. Its balanced split has 47 classes: 10 digits, 26 capitals and the 11 lowercase letters that don't look like their capitals.

In Homework 06 and 07 we train on 9,400 of these from the police archive, then point the network at the cut-out letters in Professor Dingler's note.

Backpropagation · Issues with Backprop31

Modern Momentum: ADAM

Plain gradient descent gives every weight the   α. The exam network has 79,510 weights and biases for MNIST, so weights with big, noisy gradients overshoot while weights with tiny gradients barely move. Adam (Adaptive Moment Estimation, Kingma and Ba, 2014) is the optimizer I see most today, and it fixes the step with two running averages:

m \leftarrow \beta_1\, m + (1 - \beta_1)\, \frac{\partial ℒ}{\partial \omega} v \leftarrow \beta_2\, v + (1 - \beta_2) \bp{\frac{\partial ℒ}{\partial \omega}}^2 \omega \leftarrow \omega - \alpha\, \frac{m}{\sqrt{v} + \epsilon}

In PyTorch it's one line, torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=0.001), the optimizer Homework 07's CNN trains with.

NOTE: The defaults are β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.999, and Adam also corrects m and v for starting at 0.
